Two lenses: (1) realized outcome - the player's current prospect FV minus the median FV for his pick band, with career MLB WAR shown alongside; (2) draft-day value - how many picks past his pre-draft consensus rank he was actually selected.
entries.methodology: Realized outcome bins all signed picks 2021-present into pick bands (1-5, 6-10, 11-20, 21-40, 41-75, 76-150, 151+) and takes the MEDIAN current FV in each band as the expectation for that slot; overperformance is the player's current FV minus that median. Current value is joined from the live board / debuts via the promoted- / MiLB-key link, falling back to the draft-time grade when unmatched. Draft-day value is the actual overall pick minus the pre-draft consensus rank. Players are pooled across completed classes and deduped.
entries.origin: Arkmetric, created by Noah J. Dengler, original to eephus.io.

entries.definition: Contract dollars discounted for deferral schedules at the platform 9% rate - the basis every Phase-2 market number speaks. A curated ledger (data/deferrals.json) carries the schedules: Ohtani's $700M prices as ~$197M of present liability; deals with no schedule on file keep their sticker.
entries.methodology: NPV = sum of scheduled payments / (1+0.09)^years-out, schedules rescaled to the sticker total. The 9% platform rate is deliberately harsher than the CBT's ~4.4% statutory rate, so these NPVs read lower than league-reported figures - one discount rate everywhere (prospect surplus, rational value, contracts), not a flattering per-context rate. Every guarantee >= $200M must carry a schedule or an explicit none entry (the coverage audit in the Gate-2 artifact lists misses); entries are curated-unverified until owner spot-check.
entries.origin: Arkmetric, created by Noah J. Dengler, original to eephus.io.

entries.definition: Swing-quality index from Statcast bat tracking (bat speed, swing length, attack angle/direction, swing path tilt, intercept point): how much a hitter's swing mechanics are worth, scaled so 100 = league average and higher is better. Built by Will Cahoon; eephus.io runs the model's scoring on each player's tracked MLB swings.
entries.methodology: Per-swing tracking features are filtered to competitive swings, aggregated per hitter (means + variability), and scored through the model's run-value pipelines with a reliability shrink toward 100 below ~180 swings. DATA BOUNDARY: bat tracking exists only at the MLB level (2024+); no public MiLB tracking exists, so prospects light up after debut, never before.
entries.example: A debuted prospect at Swing+ 115 with 300+ swings carries a plus swing by MLB standards; 95 on 60 swings is mostly shrink, not signal.
entries.origin: Arkmetric, created by Noah J. Dengler, original to eephus.io.

entries.definition: eephus.io's college baseball percentile module (created by Joseph Gillis): Savant-style hitter and pitcher dashboards over college TrackMan-era data, with per-metric leaderboards, player pages, and global search.
entries.methodology: Percentiles are computed within the college dataset's qualified pool per season. The module is in alpha.
entries.origin: Arkmetric, created by Noah J. Dengler, original to eephus.io.

entries.definition: eephusFV (abbreviated eFV) is our own Future Value grade and the site's PRIMARY prospect ranking, grounded in what past prospects actually became rather than in scout consensus. eFV predicts a prospect's realized first-six-MLB-season bWAR distribution and summarizes it on the 20-80 FV scale; consensus FV is shown alongside as a secondary reference. eFV needs a pro track record to grade, so very recent draftees and international signings show consensus FV until they have a season of production.
entries.methodology: eFV is a prior-anchored, outcome-grounded model. The backbone prior is consensus FV (raw, pre-rounding); a deliberately LEAN regularized model (ridge, with a guarded blend back toward consensus) nudges the grade using only the signals that actually add information beyond consensus out of sample. For hitters: level-translated on-base skill (OBP) and contact (K-rate plus its multi-season peak), an OPS-vs-level read for the fringe tiers, age relative to level and absolute age, track record (pro seasons, a missing-record indicator, IFA/college acquisition cohorts), highest level reached (proximity to the majors), and the hit and speed tools. For pitchers: multi-season peak and final-season strikeout rate, walk rate, K-backed run prevention (the x_era_k interaction behind KRP+), age relative to level and absolute age, and the fastball. Game power is deliberately excluded for hitters, because scouts over-price it relative to realized WAR - that omission is eFV's power-correction. It is trained leakage-free on prospects who debuted 2011-2024 (boards strictly before debut) against their realized 6-year bWAR, busts kept at zero, forward-chained out of time; the 2024 debut class is right-censored (two of its six seasons observed) and enters at reduced weight. The headline grade is value_framework.outcome_implied_fv(E[6yr bWAR]): the inverse of the POOLED empirical outcome curve fitted on resolved cohorts, so the number states the FV whose measured first-six-year bWAR matches this prediction. It is NOT a rank-map onto the consensus distribution; that retired per-side quantile map stopped being displayed on 2026-07-25, when the board unified on one number for display, sort and rank. Surplus dollars are still priced through the RETIRED quantile grade, deliberately, because the surplus and WAR-path curves were fitted on the consensus 20-80 scale that map lands on - which is exactly why re-anchoring the headline grade on 2026-07-30 moved zero dollars. Displayed grade and priced grade are therefore two different numbers on purpose. The star/bust outcome odds stay on the retired realized-implied map for the same reason: they were ground-truthed on it, and re-keying them has not been measured. On the live board only, owner-directed overlays (injury, prospect age, stale list coverage, and a reliever-ceiling dial) tilt the model's WAR leg and surface as labeled factor chips; the reliever ceiling is a policy dial, not an accuracy claim - relief-designated arms age 25 and up whose model WAR runs hot take a bounded haircut on the model leg (0.80, or 0.70 from age 26), because list-time relievers of that profile almost never returned star value in the resolved training rows and the survivorship-censored data cannot price that risk on its own. Measured standing, and it is a TIE rather than a win: on eFV's own out-of-sample protocol the ordering gap against consensus FV is SMALLER THAN THE MARGIN THE EVAL CAN RESOLVE on both sides, so neither grade is shown as the winner. The live figures, the noise floor and the per-era split are printed on the Methodology page and read from the backtest artifact rather than repeated here, because accuracy numbers written into copy go stale silently and this sentence previously carried three that had drifted. Split by debut era the ordering is NOT uniform: consensus leads the oldest cohort, eFV leads the most recent, and the middle cohort splits by side, so no claim is made that eFV is simply better on newer scouting. LEVEL CALIBRATION, corrected 2026-08-14: the projected WAR used to be over-dispersed out of sample, reading too extreme in both directions and implying that hundreds of prospects would produce negative six-year WAR. An affine correction fitted out of fold on eleven forward-chained folds now brings the calibration slope to about 1.0 on both sides and cuts overall absolute error, and the rows pinned at the -2.0 WAR floor fall from 117 to 13 (hitters) and 24 to 10 (pitchers). THE COST, stated because it is real and permanent: for the players who went on to be stars, the top tenth of realized outcomes, the projected WAR now reads FURTHER BELOW what they actually produced, by roughly 1.2 WAR (hitters) and 0.5 (pitchers) across six years, in exchange for the level being right everywhere else. No affine correction can fix the middle and the extreme tail at once, and fitting a second family until one passed is banned. The flagship case: the calibrated outcome distribution, the uncertainty band, and the surplus translation. Provisional. GRADE SCALE, restamped 2026-07-30: the number you see is the FV whose MEASURED first-six-year bWAR matches our prediction for this player, read off a curve fitted on prospects who were graded, then debuted, then either produced or did not. It is a pure function of predicted WAR and takes no age or position, so two players with the same projection carry the same grade. Two honest limits. Below about FV45 the measured curve is flat, so grades down there preserve ORDER but their SPACING is not outcome-calibrated and should not be read as a WAR statement. Above about FV57 the measured cells fall into single digits per grade and are blended heavily toward a published industry prior, so the very top of the board is closer to the industry's table than to our own measurement. Surplus dollars are still priced through the retired per-side quantile grade, which is why re-anchoring the grade moved no money, and the star/bust odds still sit on the retired map because they were ground-truthed on it.
entries.formula: eFV grade = outcome_implied_fv( E[6yr bWAR] ), the inverse of the pooled empirical outcome curve fitted on resolved cohorts; surplus = value_framework( retired per-side quantile grade ); star/bust odds = outcome model( retired realized-implied FV )
entries.example: A contact-and-discipline hitter consensus has at 45 can read 48 eFV when his translated MiLB walk and strikeout rates beat the level; a power-over-hit profile can read lower, since power adds less realized WAR than scouts price.
entries.origin: Arkmetric, created by Noah J. Dengler, original to eephus.io.

entries.definition: Per-tool version of eFV: each 20-80 tool re-graded by how well it plus the prospect's relevant production predicts the realized MLB outcome that tool is supposed to forecast.
entries.methodology: For each tool with a clean realized target we ground it in the MLB stat it predicts: power in MLB ISO, hit in MLB average and contact, speed in steals, the fastball in MLB strikeout rate, command in walk rate. The tool eFV blends the consensus tool grade (a strong predictor on its own) with the pre-debut MiLB production only where that production adds signal beyond the grade. In practice the scout grades are already good (power grade to MLB ISO ranks at about 0.52), and production adds most for the fastball-to-strikeout case. Tools with no clean realized metric in our data (raw power, fielding, arm, individual breaking-ball shapes) pass the consensus grade through unchanged, disclosed as such.
entries.formula: tool eFV = rank-map( z(grade) + w*z(MiLB production) ), w from the production's partial correlation after the grade
entries.example: A pitcher whose fastball grades 55 but who already misses bats at an elite MiLB rate can carry a higher fastball eFV, because realized strikeout rate adds to the grade for predicting MLB strikeouts.
entries.origin: Arkmetric, created by Noah J. Dengler, original to eephus.io.

entries.definition: A PROVISIONAL Future Value grade for prospects who have played pro ball but have NOT yet received a grade from any scouting source -- the DSL/CPX breakout bats and arms the prospect cycle is behind on, plus deep-system org depth. Shown on farm-detail rosters with a dashed badge and a small 'p', so it never reads as a real (source-anchored) eFV grade. Most land 20-30; only genuine production breakouts reach the mid-40s, where a hard cap keeps an un-scouted player from reading as a top prospect.
entries.methodology: The flagship eFV model is anchored on consensus FV and abstains when there is no source grade, so ungraded players need a dedicated, production-only model. We re-fit a ridge on the SAME translated MiLB production substrate the flagship uses (level-relative K/BB/OBP/ISO vs contemporaneous norms, age-for-level, multi-season peaks, track record) but WITHOUT the consensus-FV feature, so the production signals carry the full WAR prediction. Forward-chained out-of-sample on the low-minors cohort it ranks realized WAR about as well as scout grades do for graded low-minors players (hitters keep level reached; pitchers drop it because it rewards quad-A org arms). The WAR prediction maps through a conventional, capped, absolute grade curve calibrated so a typical org filler reads ~22-25 and a real breakout reaches the cap. It is a leading indicator -- not the flagship grade -- and is not folded into the board rank or the farm-system rank composite.
entries.formula: ungraded eFV = clamp( BASE + SLOPE * model E[6yr bWAR] , 20 , cap )  (no consensus-FV anchor; hit cap 43 / pit cap 40)
entries.example: Franklin Primera (CPX, age 19) has no source grade yet but a strong on-base line for his level -> a provisional eFV of 43, flagging him as a breakout candidate a development cycle before the boards catch up.
entries.origin: Arkmetric, created by Noah J. Dengler, original to eephus.io.

entries.definition: Pitcher index for run prevention backed by missing bats: a below-level ERA that an above-level strikeout rate supports. 100 = active-pitcher-pool average, 10 pts = 1 std-dev; higher is better.
entries.methodology:
KRP+ standardizes the eFV pitcher model's run-prevention x missing-bats interaction onto the shared '+' scale. The raw term is (-era_rel) x k_rel, a product of two exposure-shrunk level-relative rates: era_rel = ERA minus the level-median ERA (so -era_rel rewards a below-level ERA), and k_rel = K% minus the level-median K% (rewarding an above-level strikeout rate). Both are shrunk by batters faced, w = BF / (BF + 40), so a cameo collapses toward 0 and reads pool-neutral rather than extreme. (The shrink constant was 80 until the 2026-07-24c reliability loosen; it is 40 today, in efv_dataset._season_rates.) The product is high only when both legs hold, i.e. the run prevention is K-backed (a skill signal) rather than a low ERA on weak contact (a luck signal).

THE DISPLAY PILL AND THE MODEL FEATURE DELIBERATELY DIFFER, and here is exactly how. When BOTH legs are bad (ERA worse than level AND K% below level) the raw product of two negatives would read positive. The eFV MODEL feature (efv_model._x_era_k) ZEROES that double-bad quadrant rather than crediting it (2026-07-14 owner-directed correction), which is correct for the fit but collapses roughly 834 doubly-below-average arms onto a single flat value that reads league-average. So the DISPLAY pill (efv_score._krp_display_raw, owner-authorized 2026-07-24) keeps the same value in every other quadrant and instead carries the negatively-signed magnitude there, so those arms spread below the pool by severity. The model keeps the zero; the pill does not; nothing else diverges. For the display raw only, era_rel is first winsorized to plus or minus 6 so a one-inning ERA blowup cannot drive the pill.

The display raw is then z-scored over the live pitcher pool and anchored at 100 + 10z (population sigma, the same convention as SC+, DvM+ and pStuff+), with no clamp (the old 40-160 display clamp was removed 2026-07-24b; see the plus_metric_recal registry row). Pitchers only, and only when innings are on file. It is the standalone reading of the signal that also drives the 'K-backed run prevention' factor in the eFV explainer.
entries.formula:
KRP+ = 100 + 10 x (x_display - pool_mean) / pool_sd over the live pitcher pool, population sigma, no clamp.
x_display = (-era_rel) x k_rel everywhere EXCEPT the double-bad quadrant (era_rel > 0 AND k_rel < 0), where x_display = -abs((-era_rel) x k_rel).
MODEL feature (the eFV input, efv_model._x_era_k) = the same product except the double-bad quadrant returns 0.0. The pill and the model feature agree everywhere else.
era_rel and k_rel are level-relative rates shrunk by BF / (BF + 40); for the display raw only, era_rel is winsorized to plus or minus 6.
entries.example: A AA starter at a 2.90 ERA (level 4.20) with a 29% K% (level 22%) posts a strongly positive x_era_k, a low ERA his strikeouts support, and reads KRP+ ~120. The same 2.90 ERA on a 19% K% reads near 100: run prevention the peripherals do not back.

entries.definition: Top-level module to value a trade both ways in one surplus currency: prospects priced on eFV surplus (calibrated control-window NPV), MLB players on projection surplus (NPV of projected production minus salary over salary-known seasons). Build a package per side; the verdict reads net surplus, with a $5M dead-band for 'balanced'.
entries.methodology: The module pairs a build-a-package evaluator with the Bayesian trade-value board. Each player carries the SAME surplus the rest of the site shows: a prospect's eFV-driven control-window surplus (value_mm) or an MLB player's projection surplus (proj.surNpv, the MLB Projections engine's NPV of convex production value minus salary on salary-known seasons). That shared currency is what lets a prospect and a veteran sit on one ledger. Cross-links run both ways: an MLB Projections player page deep-links into the evaluator and pre-loads that player; evaluator rows link back to the player's projections / prospect page. The 'balanced' dead-band is $5M, shared with the Transactions Trade Audit so the two never disagree. Board ranks are contract-aware (surplus over remaining controlled years), positional-scarcity and opt-out adjusted. Module by Anirudh Iyer.

entries.definition: A hitting prospect's projected first-MLB-season K% and BB%, translated from his final pre-debut level-relative MiLB rate. K% is the reliable read (2026-08 fit: r2 0.32); BB% is modest and flagged. Production (OPS/xwOBA) does not translate across the jump and is deliberately not projected.
entries.methodology: Matched-pair regression-to-the-mean (the CollegeSavant college-to-Single-A method, applied MiLB-to-MLB): each debuted hitter's final pre-debut level-relative rate (k_rel / bb_rel vs the level mean) is paired with his realized first-MLB-season rate, and a shrunk slope is fit over the pairs. Leave-one-out validated, 2026-08 fit (n=287): K% LOO MAE 3.9, P10-P90 coverage 0.81, r2 0.32; BB% MAE 2.7, coverage 0.78, r2 0.14 (flagged with *). These are dated readings of the validation block in data/milb_translation.json and move with each refit. The band is the residual spread. OPS / xwOBA were tested and do NOT translate (r2 ~0.02): first-MLB production level is selection/survivorship-dominated, so only the sticky plate-skill rates are projected. Descriptive rate translation, not a value forecast; eFV is the prospect-to-MLB value signal.

entries.definition: A reliever's run-prevention skill on a league-relative scale where 100 is an average reliever and 110 is 10 percent better. Built from stabilized strikeout, walk, and contact-quality rates, regressed for small samples, and anchored to the reliever-only pool. Higher is better.
entries.methodology: REM+ is a FIP-based skill rate on the ERA+ family, a ratio to the league rather than a z-score. The component rates (K%, BB%, HBP, and a heavily regressed home-run rate) are each shrunk toward the reliever pool mean by sample size, then combined into a sample-shrunk FIP. REM+ = 100 times the pool-average FIP divided by the reliever's FIP, so a lower FIP scores above 100. The pool mean is taken over relievers only, so 100 is the average reliever, not the average pitcher. Leverage is left out of the number on purpose: gmLI, WPA, and Shutdowns minus Meltdowns ride separate Impact columns, because reliever leverage is assigned by the manager and does not carry forward as a repeatable skill.
entries.formula: REM+ = 100 x poolFIP / playerFIP (sample-shrunk FIP; 100 = average reliever)
entries.origin: Arkmetric, created by Noah J. Dengler, original to eephus.io.

entries.definition: A team bullpen rating where 100 is an average pen. A relief-innings-weighted blend of the pen's relievers' REM+, so it reads the talent of the innings a bullpen actually throws.
entries.methodology: Bullpen+ weights each reliever's REM+ by his relief innings, so a pen is credited for the quality of the innings it throws, not for how its manager assigns leverage. A separate Leverage Deployment number weights by innings times gmLI, showing how much leverage those innings carried. Alongside it the board shows bullpen depth (the share of above-average arms) and a high-leverage core rating (the top arms by entry leverage).
entries.origin: Arkmetric, created by Noah J. Dengler, original to eephus.io.

entries.definition: A team rotation rating where 100 is an average rotation. A starter-innings-weighted blend of the staff's SEM+, so it reads the run-prevention talent of the innings a rotation actually starts. Shown on the Team Rotations board in MLB Stats. Higher is better.
entries.methodology: Rotation+ weights each starter's SEM+ by the innings he threw as a starter, then divides by those same innings, so a staff is credited for the quality of the innings it actually covers instead of the length of its depth chart: a swingman with 30 innings cannot move a rotation the way a flat average would let him. Only starters carrying a scored SEM+ and positive innings enter the weight, and the result is rounded to a whole point for display (the unrounded value ships alongside it as rotation_plus_raw). Because SEM+ is anchored over the starter pool, 100 is the average ROTATION, not the average staff, and Rotation+ inherits SEM+'s sample shrinkage rather than adding any of its own. Nothing else is mixed in: Front 3 (the mean SEM+ of the three best starters, reading the top of the rotation), the count of above-average starters, and the durability columns (starter innings, games started) sit beside the rating as context and never enter it. Built by starter_export.py, which feeds the StatsAPI season pitching leaderboard into sem_plus.score_pool and rolls up sem_plus.team_rotation per club.
entries.formula: Rotation+ = sum(SEM+ x starter IP) / sum(starter IP), over starters with a scored SEM+ (100 = average rotation)
entries.origin: Arkmetric, created by Noah J. Dengler, original to eephus.io.

entries.definition: A team lineup rating where 100 is an average offense. A plate-appearance-weighted blend of the club's HEM+, so it reads the offensive quality of the plate appearances a lineup actually takes. Shown on the Team Lineups board in MLB Stats. Higher is better.
entries.methodology: Offense+ weights each hitter's HEM+ by his plate appearances and divides by those same plate appearances, so playing time decides how much a bat counts toward the club number without playing time entering the rate itself: a hot bench bat with 40 trips cannot carry a lineup. Only hitters with a scored HEM+ and positive PA enter the weight, and the result is rounded to a whole point for display (the unrounded value ships alongside it as offense_plus_raw). Because HEM+ is anchored over the hitter pool, 100 is the average LINEUP, not the average hitter. It rides the same WIDER spread HEM+ displays on: HEM+ is stretched from the bare wOBA ratio to the wRC+ deviation width by a fixed monotone gain, so read Offense+ against roughly 16 points per standard deviation rather than the tighter REM+/SEM+ bands. Heart 3 (the top three regulars by HEM+), the count of above-average hitters, and team PA sit beside the rating as context and never enter it; the constructed batting orders versus right- and left-handed pitching and the bench list are display only. Built by hitter_export.py, which feeds the StatsAPI season hitting leaderboard into hem_plus.score_pool and rolls up hem_plus.team_offense per club.
entries.formula: Offense+ = sum(HEM+ x PA) / sum(PA), over hitters with a scored HEM+ (100 = average lineup)

entries.definition: A fielder's sprint speed expressed as a range read on the 100 + 10z scale, where 100 is the league average position player and ten points is one standard deviation. It appears as a chip on the Position Fit rows in the Pitcher Alchemy Lab, and ONLY on left-field and centre-field destinations. It is display only: it never enters the position-fit model.
entries.methodology:
Sprint speed comes from the Statcast leaderboard for the current season, falling back one season when a player has no current tracking (the chip labels the season it read). It is standardized against that season's MLB position-player pool, so Rng+ = 100 + 10 x z(feet per second), and the chip also reports the player's percentile among incumbents at the destination position, meaning everyone with 400 or more innings there over the trailing three seasons.

The whitelist is the finding, not caution about it. Measured against OAA per 1000 innings at the position played (400+ innings, 2016-2026), sprint speed tracks range in centre field at r = +0.428 (95 percent CI +0.342 to +0.507) and in left field at r = +0.416 (+0.323 to +0.501), so those two destinations ship the chip. Right field clears the headline bar at r = +0.269 (+0.167 to +0.365) but is EXCLUDED, because that signal is carried by displaced centre fielders: right fielders with under 100 career centre-field innings come back at r = +0.075 (-0.111 to +0.256), whose lower bound sits below the +0.15 bar, so the chip would be telling corner-only right fielders something never measured on players like them. Left field survives the identical pure-corner test (+0.359, +0.163 to +0.528, n = 89). Shortstop (-0.020, -0.122 to +0.083) and third base (-0.004, -0.108 to +0.100) have no signal at all, so a speed meter on an infield row would be a picture of a measured zero and is never rendered.

Nothing here reaches the model: positional_fit's field() carries no sprint term, because OAA already contains the legs and a sprint feature would double-count it. That is the same argument that rejected the arm feature. The producer (build_site.py) decides which positions qualify and bakes every number, including the per-destination percentile; assets/pal.js computes none of it and renders no chip for a position off the whitelist.
entries.formula: Rng+ = 100 + 10 x z(sprint speed, ft/s) against the current-season MLB position-player pool; shipped for LF and CF destinations only

entries.definition: The average Leverage Index at the moment a reliever enters the game. A measure of how high-pressure his usage is, set largely by the manager, not the pitcher. About 1.0 is average; closers run high, mop-up arms run low.
entries.methodology: Computed in house from the MLB win-probability feed: for each appearance, the Leverage Index of the play where the reliever enters is recorded, and gmLI is the average across his appearances. It captures deployment, not skill, which is why REM+ keeps it in a separate column.
entries.origin: Arkmetric, created by Noah J. Dengler, original to eephus.io.

entries.definition: The relief-entry-weighted average gmLI a pitcher's managers assigned him over the trailing three seasons, shown with his pool percentile. Deployment context, not skill: it says how he has been used, not how well he pitched. About 1.0 is average; established high-leverage arms run 1.5 and up.
entries.methodology:
Each season's gmLI (entry-point Leverage Index, computed in house from the MLB win-probability feed) is averaged across the trailing three seasons, weighted by relief entries. The multi-year framing is gate-validated: year-over-year gmLI rank correlation on qualified relievers is 0.47 pooled over 2018-2025 (excluding 2020), with within-season split-half stability of 0.53, so a manager's leverage assignment is a persistent trait worth displaying.

Players with fewer than 2 seasons or 60 relief entries in the window carry a provisional mark. gmLI 3yr never feeds REM+, which deliberately excludes leverage from the skill scale.
entries.origin: Arkmetric, created by Noah J. Dengler, original to eephus.io.

entries.definition: The realized leverage-weighted VALUE a reliever produced this season, on a 100-anchored scale (100 = average, higher is more value). RIV+ is the deployment-value companion to REM+: where REM+ is pure run-prevention skill with leverage held out, RIV+ credits the wins a reliever actually added in the leverage he was given. An elite high-leverage closer scores far above his own REM+; a good arm used in low-leverage work scores below it.
entries.methodology:
RIV+ standardizes a WPA-primary composite over the season's reliever pool and reports it as 100 plus ten times the standard score. The composite is 70 percent Win Probability Added (WPA already weights every out by the leverage of the moment) and 30 percent shutdowns minus meltdowns (a lower-variance count of the high-impact good and bad outings). Leverage enters only through the value a reliever produced, never as free credit for being handed a high-leverage role.

RIV+ is a realized-VALUE measure, not a repeatable-skill number. By design it is less stable year to year than REM+: its year-over-year rank correlation is 0.21 versus 0.35 for REM+ over 2018-2025 (excluding 2020), which is exactly why leverage stays out of the REM+ skill scale and rides here instead. RIV+ tracks what teams pay relief free agents at least as closely as REM+ does. Accountability artifact: data/riv_plus_eval.json.
entries.origin: Arkmetric, created by Noah J. Dengler, original to eephus.io.

entries.definition: REM+ over the trailing three seasons, innings-weighted, shown with the pitcher's pool percentile. Same pure-skill run-prevention scale as REM+ (100 = average reliever). Read it as a steadier version of the single-season number, not a stronger forecast.
entries.methodology: Each of the trailing three seasons' REM+ is averaged with innings-pitched weights. Single reliever seasons are volatile (within-season split-half REM+ correlation only about 0.34 at 100 to 150 batters faced), so a three-year window is a more stable talent read. It did NOT beat the single-season number in the forward test: three-year forward Spearman 0.237 versus 0.232 for one year, and the difference is not statistically separable (95% interval on the gap runs negative). So it ships as a steadiness companion, not a more predictive column.
entries.origin: Arkmetric, created by Noah J. Dengler, original to eephus.io.

entries.definition: A starting pitcher's run-prevention skill on a 100-anchored scale (100 = the average qualified starter, 110 = 10 percent better run prevention). The starter cousin of REM+: a sample-shrunk, starter-pool-anchored FIP built from strikeouts, walks, hit batters, and a heavily regressed home-run rate. Durability (innings, games started, average start length) is shown alongside as context, never mixed into the skill number.
entries.methodology:
Each rate is regressed toward the starter-pool average by sample size (the same empirical-Bayes recipe REM+ uses), turned into a fielding-independent ERA, and expressed as 100 times the pool-average skill FIP over the pitcher's own. The pool is re-normalized over starters, so 100 is the average starter, not the average pitcher.

Validated out of sample: forward-chained over 2018-2025 (excluding 2020), SEM+ predicts a starter's next-year runs-allowed rate at a Spearman correlation of 0.39, beating ERA (0.26; gap confidence floor above zero) and edging its raw-FIP parent (0.36), so the shrinkage and starter anchoring earn their place. A ground-ball-adjusted variant was tested and did not beat plain FIP out of sample, so the plain core ships. Quality starts and times-through-order are not in the source feed, so average start length carries the durability read. Accountability artifact: data/sem_plus_eval.json.
entries.origin: Arkmetric, created by Noah J. Dengler, original to eephus.io.

entries.definition: A hitter's offensive-rate skill on a 100-anchored scale (100 = the average qualified hitter), scaled to the wRC+ convention so the league reads with real separation (about 15 points per standard deviation). The hitter cousin of REM+/SEM+: a sample-shrunk, hitter-pool-anchored wOBA built from unintentional walks, hit-by-pitches, singles, doubles, triples, and home runs. Volume (plate appearances), baserunning (steals), and the slash line are shown alongside as context, never mixed into the skill number.
entries.methodology:
Each wOBA component rate is regressed toward the hitter-pool average by sample size (the same empirical-Bayes recipe REM+ uses, with a slower pull for the extra-base hits that stabilize late), recombined with the FanGraphs wOBA linear weights, and re-anchored over hitters so the pool average scores 100; HEM+ = 100 times the shrunk player wOBA over the pool wOBA, a ratio-to-league index in the wRC+/OPS+ family, not a z-score.

Validated out of sample: forward-chained over 2012-2024 (excluding 2020), HEM+ predicts a hitter's next-year wOBA at a Spearman correlation of 0.41, decisively beating batting average (0.23; gap confidence floor well above zero) and holding even-or-ahead of its raw-wOBA parent (0.41), so the component shrinkage and hitter anchoring earn their place. Volume, baserunning, and defense are separate value and stay out of the rate number. Accountability artifact: data/hem_plus_eval.json. Display scale: the score is stretched from the bare wOBA ratio to the wRC+ deviation width by a fixed monotone gain (HEM_SPREAD_GAIN), which preserves player RANK exactly (so the validation is unchanged) while giving the league visible spread.
entries.origin: Arkmetric, created by Noah J. Dengler, original to eephus.io.

entries.definition: A hitter's HEM+ over the trailing three seasons (plate-appearance-weighted), a steadier read on offensive-rate talent than a single season. Same 100-anchored scale as HEM+.
entries.methodology: The PA-weighted mean of the hitter's HEM+ across the last three seasons (2024-2026), so a partial current season is weighted by its plate appearances and the fuller prior seasons carry more. 'Established' means 2+ seasons and 600+ PA in the window; below that it is flagged provisional. Validated out of sample: forward-chained over 2012-2024 (ex-2020), the 3-year read predicts next-year wOBA at a Spearman correlation of 0.45 vs 0.43 for a single season on the same hitters, with the same-set gap confidence floor above zero -- so more sample is a genuinely steadier talent estimate (a stronger result than the SEM+ 3yr case). Accountability artifact: data/hem_plus_multiyear_eval.json.
entries.origin: Arkmetric, created by Noah J. Dengler, original to eephus.io.

entries.definition: WAR/PA+ with the rate regressed toward the league rate by how many plate appearances the hitter actually took, so a hot hundred-plate-appearance line does not outrank a strong full season. Same 100-anchored, ten-points-per-standard-deviation scale, rebuilt on the regressed pool. Use it to read the board; use plain WAR/PA+ to read what a hitter banked.
entries.methodology:
The same WAR/PA+ with one change made first: the rate is pulled toward the pool rate in proportion to how little the player played, using the pool's median plate-appearance count as the halfway point, and only then indexed. A player at that median sits halfway between his own rate and the league's; a full season barely moves; a player just over the display gate moves a long way. It exists because the unadjusted column ranks a hot short sample above a good full season, which is true of what was banked but is not what most readers are asking when they sort the board.

The scale is rebuilt on the regressed pool, not borrowed from the unregressed one, so ten points is still one standard deviation of the hitter pool. Doing it the other way is a real and previously shipped defect: an index that shrinks its numerator but keeps the old spread quietly stops being the scale it advertises.

What it is not: a forecast. On the forward test the pre-registered shrink rule fired for this pool, with a paired gap of 0.0148 (95 percent interval 0.01 to 0.0195), and a volume control shows where that gap comes from. Splitting the same players into thirds by playing time, the gap survives in high, so most of the pooled improvement is the shrink standing in for sample size rather than measuring skill better. Read this column as the readable version of the rate, the unadjusted one as the banked truth, and neither as a projection. Measurement ledger: data/war_rate_plus_eval.json.

entries.definition: Starter WAR/IP+ with the rate regressed toward the starter pool rate by innings pitched, so a short hot stretch does not outrank a full season. entries.definition: How much total value a hitter banked per trip to the plate, on a 100-anchored scale where ten points is one standard deviation of the hitter pool. Batting bWAR divided by plate appearances. It answers a different question from HEM+: HEM+ is offensive rate alone, while WAR/PA+ carries fielding, baserunning and the positional adjustment, so a good defender at a hard position can sit well above his HEM+ and a designated hitter well below it. Needs 100 plate appearances to show.
entries.methodology:
Anchored at 100 with ten points per standard deviation of the anchor pool, which is hitters with 50 or more plate appearances. That is a different ruler from the HEM+ / SEM+ / REM+ columns beside it: those are ratios to the pool average, where a point is about one percent. Ten WAR-rate points is one full standard deviation, so 120 is a top-2.5-percent season and 80 is a bottom-2.5-percent one. A ratio index cannot be built here at all, because the league average WAR per plate appearance is a hair above zero and individual values go negative, so dividing by the pool average would flip sign and blow up. Ten points per standard deviation is the only honest scale for a signed near-zero-mean rate.

Two volume floors, doing two different jobs. Everyone at or above the pool floor sets the pool average and spread; only players at or above 100 plate appearances get a published value, so a brief hot stretch cannot print a number. The value is not shrunk toward the average and not clamped at either end, so what you read is what the player actually banked, including the tail. Right at the display gate the sample is still small, which is why the default board view also applies its usual qualified filter.

Source: Baseball-Reference WAR (bWAR), the site-wide WAR standard, with the batting and pitching sides read from separate keys so the two are never summed onto one number. Two-way players are handled by keeping the two sides of bWAR apart rather than by any discount factor. Batting WAR is divided by plate appearances on the hitter board and pitching WAR by innings on a pitcher board, so a two-way player carries two different indexes on two different boards and both are correct.

Forward-checked out of sample, and it lost. Over 2012-2025 (excluding 2020) and 3845 year-to-year pairs, WAR/PA+ predicts next season's WAR rate at a Spearman correlation of 0.3711, while plain season bWAR with no rate at all predicts the same thing at 0.4058. It is not noise: a zero-information control on the same pairs scores 0.0011, so the number carries real signal about the player. It simply does not forecast better than the plainest alternative, because a season of playing time is itself a talent signal that a per-trip rate throws away. So this is registered as a descriptive display index with no validated verdict and no eval artifact attached, rather than dressed up with a backtest it did not pass. Read it as what a player banked, not as a forecast. Measurement ledger: data/war_rate_plus_eval.json.
entries.origin: Arkmetric, created by Noah J. Dengler, original to eephus.io.

entries.definition: A hitter's WAR/PA+ over the trailing three seasons, weighted by plate appearances. Steadier than one season, because a WAR rate carries fielding and baserunning on top of the bat and all three bounce around in a single year. Same 100-anchored, ten-points-per-standard-deviation scale as WAR/PA+.
entries.methodology:
The plate-appearance-weighted mean of the player's single-season WAR/PA+ across the trailing three seasons, so a partial current season counts for what it is worth and the fuller prior seasons carry more. Established means two or more seasons and 600 plate appearances in the window; below that the value is marked provisional with a star.

This column is a FROZEN vintage, not a live number. The values are read verbatim from data/war_rate_plus_multiyear_eval.json and are never recomputed when the board is built, so a row can show a same-day one-year value beside a three-year value frozen weeks earlier, and a player who entered the pool after that file was generated is simply blank. The board payload carries the generation date so the gap is visible rather than silent.

Forward-checked: over 3845 pairs the three-year read predicts next season's WAR rate at a Spearman correlation of 0.4022 against 0.3711 for a single season on the same players, with the paired gap confidence floor above zero, so more sample really is a steadier read.
entries.origin: Arkmetric, created by Noah J. Dengler, original to eephus.io.

entries.definition: How much value a starting pitcher banked per inning, on a 100-anchored scale where ten points is one standard deviation of the STARTER pool. Pitching bWAR divided by innings pitched, anchored on starters only. It reads run prevention and workload together, where SEM+ is run-prevention rate alone. It does not compare with the reliever board's WAR/IP+: relievers bank more WAR per inning than starters of equal talent, so the two boards are anchored on separate pools and are never pooled into one ranking. Needs 40 innings to show.
entries.methodology:
Anchored at 100 with ten points per standard deviation of the anchor pool, which is starters with 20 or more innings. That is a different ruler from the HEM+ / SEM+ / REM+ columns beside it: those are ratios to the pool average, where a point is about one percent. Ten WAR-rate points is one full standard deviation, so 120 is a top-2.5-percent season and 80 is a bottom-2.5-percent one. A ratio index cannot be built here at all, because the league average WAR per inning is a hair above zero and individual values go negative, so dividing by the pool average would flip sign and blow up. Ten points per standard deviation is the only honest scale for a signed near-zero-mean rate.

Two volume floors, doing two different jobs. Everyone at or above the pool floor sets the pool average and spread; only players at or above 40 innings get a published value, so a brief hot stretch cannot print a number. The value is not shrunk toward the average and not clamped at either end, so what you read is what the player actually banked, including the tail. Right at the display gate the sample is still small, which is why the default board view also applies its usual qualified filter.

Source: Baseball-Reference WAR (bWAR), the site-wide WAR standard, with the batting and pitching sides read from separate keys so the two are never summed onto one number. Two-way players are handled by keeping the two sides of bWAR apart rather than by any discount factor. Batting WAR is divided by plate appearances on the hitter board and pitching WAR by innings on a pitcher board, so a two-way player carries two different indexes on two different boards and both are correct.

Forward-checked out of sample, and it lost. Over 2012-2025 (excluding 2020) and 1396 year-to-year pairs, starter WAR/IP+ predicts next season's WAR rate at a Spearman correlation of 0.2688, while plain season bWAR with no rate at all predicts the same thing at 0.2799. It is not noise: a zero-information control on the same pairs scores 0.0502, so the number carries real signal about the player. It simply does not forecast better than the plainest alternative, because a season of playing time is itself a talent signal that a per-trip rate throws away. So this is registered as a descriptive display index with no validated verdict and no eval artifact attached, rather than dressed up with a backtest it did not pass. Read it as what a player banked, not as a forecast. Measurement ledger: data/war_rate_plus_eval.json.

entries.definition: A starter's WAR/IP+ over the trailing three seasons, weighted by innings. Same starter-anchored, ten-points-per-standard-deviation scale as WAR/IP+, over a longer window.

It is offered as a longer window on the same scale, not as a better forecast.
